The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — [P2, confidence 75] `record.save`: coupling optional telemetry persistence to the policy predicate makes a lock timeout or write failure abort a configured `do_nothing` match before the allow decision is returned, rejecting a signup solely because statistics could not be recorded.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in BlockedEmail.should_block?, the record.save call happens before the return statement that determines whether to block. If save fails (due to lock timeout, write failure, etc.), it could raise an exception that would abort the method before returning the allow/block decision. For action_type == :do_nothing, this means a user who should be allowed through could be rejected because the statistics update failed. The code at lines 12-17 shows: record.match_count += 1, record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now, record.save, then return record && record.action_type == actions[:block]. A save failure would prevent reaching the return statement.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:5 — [P2, confidence 100] `t.integer :action_type, null: false`: the schema accepts every integer while `record.action_type == actions[:block]` treats every unknown value as allow, so one malformed import value silently disables blocking for that address.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue. In BlockedEmail.should_block?, the method returns `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`. This means any action_type value other than the specific :block enum value (including invalid integers from malformed imports) will return false, effectively allowing the email through. The schema only enforces NOT NULL but accepts any integer, so invalid values would silently disable blocking. This is a correctness bug where data integrity issues could lead to security bypass.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:5 — [P3, confidence 75] `t.integer :action_type, null: false`: the database omits the model's block-by-default value, so the direct/manual blocklist loads anticipated by the feature fail the NOT NULL constraint unless each writer duplicates the model-only default.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue. The migration creates the `action_type` column with `null: false` but no default value at the database level. The model's `set_defaults` callback only sets `self.action_type ||= BlockedEmail.actions[:block]` before validation, which works for records created through ActiveRecord. However, as the finding notes, direct SQL inserts or bulk loads (which the spec comments suggest are anticipated: 'If we manually load the table with some emails...') would fail the NOT NULL constraint since there's no database-level default. This is a legitimate defect where the database schema doesn't match the intended behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — [P2, confidence 100] `record.match_count += 1`: every blocked signup increments `match_count` twice because `UsersController#create` invokes `user.valid?` and then `user.save` re-runs validation, so the statistics report two matches for one attempt.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real bug. Looking at the diff: 1) EmailValidator's validate_each method calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) which increments match_count. 2) The User model has 'validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?' which triggers this validator. 3) In Rails, when UsersController#create calls user.save, validations run. If the controller also explicitly calls user.valid? before save (common pattern), or if save runs validations twice internally, the counter would increment multiple times. The finding correctly identifies that the statistics tracking in should_block? (incrementing match_count and saving) will be called each time validation runs, leading to inflated counts. This is a legitimate correctness bug in the statistics tracking logic.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that `record.save` in `should_block?` (line 16) could fail silently if validations fail, causing match_count and last_match_at updates to be lost while still returning the block decision. adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — [P3, confidence 75] `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])`: this mutable prototype array is shared by every controller instance, so an address rejected in one signup controller remains client-side invalid in later instances and cannot be retried against changed server state; singleton controller usage only hides the contamination until another instance is created.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined as a mutable array on the controller's prototype. In Ember.js, when you define an array or object directly on the prototype like this, all instances share the same reference. This means if an email is rejected and added to `rejectedEmails` via `pushObject(result.values.email)` (line 274), that email will remain in the shared array and be considered invalid for all future controller instances. The diff shows this array is used to check if emails should be blocked client-side (lines 68-74), so this is a real bug where rejected emails persist incorrectly across controller instances.
